concepts.decision: Create a zone when its trust requirement differs; document crossings and exceptions.
concepts.definition: Grouping with a stated trust/business purpose, assets, identities, permitted flows, owners, and failure consequences.
concepts.failureExample: An undefined “secure zone” cannot support consistent allow/deny decisions.
concepts.label: Trust Zone

concepts.decision: Place enforcement on real crossings and test allowed, denied, and failure behavior.
concepts.definition: Physical or logical restriction of communication between zones to reduce reachability and blast radius.
concepts.failureExample: A segmented diagram with an unfiltered routing path leaves lateral movement intact.
concepts.label: Network Segmentation

concepts.decision: Use for high-value or mixed-trust workloads; maintain service identity, policy lifecycle, and telemetry.
concepts.definition: Workload/identity-level policy that limits east-west communication beyond coarse network zones.
concepts.failureExample: One compromised pod reaches peer services because the whole subnet is allowed.
concepts.label: Micro Segmentation

concepts.decision: Inventory before policy; remove stale flows and verify dependency changes.
concepts.definition: Specified source, destination, service, direction, identity, and path relationships that a zone policy evaluates.
concepts.failureExample: A forgotten backup path becomes an unmonitored bridge across zones.
concepts.label: Traffic Flows

concepts.decision: Apply explicit verification and least privilege at each requested resource/action while planning availability and telemetry.
concepts.definition: Design approach that continuously evaluates identity, device/context, and policy rather than assuming network location grants trust.
concepts.failureExample: A user on a corporate subnet receives broad access because location is treated as sufficient trust.
concepts.label: Zero Trust

concepts.decision: Use with inter-VLAN routing/ACL policy, trunk controls, management protection, and monitoring.
concepts.definition: Layer-2 logical LAN segmentation on switching infrastructure.
concepts.failureExample: Putting systems in different VLANs without controlling the router between them does not block communication.
concepts.label: Vlan

concepts.decision: Verify authentication, endpoint trust, split/full routing, authorization, logs, and termination boundary.
concepts.definition: Protected logical tunnel connecting users/sites/networks through defined endpoints and traffic selectors.
concepts.failureExample: A VPN grants a remote device broad internal reachability despite lacking device posture.
concepts.label: VPN

concepts.decision: Use for tenant/site separation while controlling route leaking, management, and monitoring.
concepts.definition: Virtual routing/forwarding instances that keep route tables and forwarding domains logically separate.
concepts.failureExample: An unintended route leak connects two customer/zone routing domains.
concepts.label: Vrf

concepts.decision: Use only with controlled transfer, maintenance, media, and verification procedures; validate no hidden bridge exists.
concepts.definition: Physical/logical separation intended to remove ordinary network paths between environments.
concepts.failureExample: A dual-homed maintenance laptop silently bridges an “air-gapped” environment.
concepts.label: Air Gap

misconceptions.claim: A perimeter firewall proves internal trust zones are effective.
misconceptions.correction: East-west movement, cloud overlays, wireless, and management paths require internal enforcement and monitoring.
Unusable complexity creates exceptions and blind spots; zones must correspond to risk and operating ownership.

outcome: Design trust zones and segmentation controls for a network scenario, justify the boundary type, and identify bypass and failure evidence.

sections.body: Inventory north-south and east-west flows, data classification, identities, service dependencies, management paths, and failure consequences. Define zones by a meaningful trust or business purpose, then choose physical, logical, or workload-level boundaries. Physical separation or an air gap reduces available paths; VLANs, VPNs, and VRF reduce logical reachability; micro-segmentation applies finer workload and identity policy.
keyPoints: The owner of a zone defines allowed purposes and evidence.
Segmentation should be based on risk and flow requirements, not topology fashion.
A boundary is incomplete if alternate routes or management paths bypass it.
sections.title: Start with flows and trust

sections.body: Place enforcement where traffic actually crosses, authenticate administrative and service identities, log allowed and denied flows, and test fail-open/fail-closed behavior. Distributed firewalls, routers, IDS/IPS, overlays, and zero-trust policy can complement zones, but each introduces configuration, availability, and observability dependencies. Review rules for stale exceptions and unintended transitive trust.
keyPoints: A segmentation design needs an explicit bypass and failure strategy.
Telemetry should reveal lateral movement and policy drift.
Zero trust continuously evaluates context; it does not make segmentation unnecessary.
sections.title: Enforce, observe, and test the boundary

teaching.scenario: A research workstation needs one analytics operation against production. The approved route crosses a policy enforcement point into a broker, which uses a scoped service identity. Administrators use a separate logged management zone. A backup appliance on that management subnet can also reach production directly through a stale broad exception.

title: Design network segmentation and trust zones

workedExamples.reasoning: Create separate research, production, and management zones; permit only documented brokered flows; use identity-aware controls and time-limited administration; monitor east-west traffic; test the design under compromised research-host and control-plane failure scenarios.
workedExamples.situation: A research network needs limited access to production analytics, while administrators require separate management access.
workedExamples.takeaway: Create separate research, production, and management zones; permit only documented brokered flows; use identity-aware controls and time-limited administration; monitor east-west traffic; test the design under compromised research-host and control-plane failure scenarios.
